title: Bekhorot 34
description: The dispute over a barrel of teruma in doubt is traced to “My terumot,” Shmuel’s ruling is pinned to Rabbi Shimon of the baraita, and the mishna on one who slits a firstborn’s ear opens a discussion of penalties: forever or until another blemish, the excised leprous mark, the bridegroom’s seven days, and whether a penalty passes to the son.

a1.he: אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא יִתֵּן בּוֹ מוּם, מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא יָבִיא דְּבֵילָה וּבָצֵק וְיַנִּיחֶנָּה עַל הָאוֹזֶן כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּבֹא כֶּלֶב וְיֹאכְלֶנָּה? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״כׇּל מוּם״ — אֶחָד מוּם וְאֶחָד כׇּל מוּם.

a2.he: הָכָא בִּקְרָאֵי פְּלִיגִי, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל, וְכֵן אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְכֵן אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ: ״וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֶת מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמֹתָי״.

a3.he: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר סָבַר: בִּשְׁתֵּי תְּרוּמוֹת הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר, אַחַת תְּרוּמָה טְהוֹרָה וְאַחַת תְּרוּמָה תְּלוּיָה, וְאָמַר רַחֲמָנָא: עֲבֵיד לַהּ שִׁימּוּר. וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: ״תְּרוּמָתִי״ כְּתִיב.

a4.he: לְמֵימְרָא דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר סָבַר יֵשׁ אֵם לַמִּקְרָא? וּרְמִינְהִי: ״בְּבִגְדוֹ בָּהּ״ — כֵּיוָן שֶׁפֵּירַשׂ טַלִּיתוֹ עָלֶיהָ, שׁוּב אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לְמוֹכְרָהּ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא.

a5.he: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּגַד בָּהּ, שׁוּב אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לְמוֹכְרָהּ!

a6.he: אֶלָּא, הָכָא בְּהָא קָמִיפַּלְגִי: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ סָבַר: הָרְאוּיָה לָךְ שְׁמוֹר, וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ רְאוּיָה לָךְ לָא תִּשְׁמוֹר, וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: הָא נָמֵי רְאוּיָה הִיא, שֶׁמָּא יָבוֹא אֵלִיָּהוּ וִיטַהֲרֶנָּה.

a7.he: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן. מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: הֵי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן? אִילֵימָא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּמַתְנִיתִין, עַד הַשְׁתָּא לָא אַשְׁמְעִינַן שְׁמוּאֵל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין מוּתָּר?

a8.he: וְהָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וְרַב חָנִין בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְרַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין מַתְנֵי בְּלָא גַּבְרֵי — רַב אָמַר: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן!

a9.he: אֶלָּא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּבָרַיְיתָא, וְרַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי מַתְנֵי לַהּ בְּהֶדְיָא: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּבָרַיְיתָא.

a10.he: מַתְנִי׳ הַצּוֹרֵם אוֹזֶן בַּבְּכוֹר — הֲרֵי זֶה לֹא יִשְׁחוֹט עוֹלָמִית, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר. וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: נוֹלַד בּוֹ מוּם אַחֵר — יִשְׁחוֹט עָלָיו.

a11.he: גְּמָ׳ וּמִי קָנֵיס רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר לְעוֹלָם? וּרְמִינְהִי: מִי שֶׁהָיְתָה לוֹ בַּהֶרֶת

b1.he: וְנִקְצְצָה — טָהוֹר, קְצָצָה מִתְכַּוֵּין — רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: לִכְשֶׁיִּוָּלֵד לוֹ נֶגַע אַחֵר יִטְהַר הֵימֶנּוּ.

b2.he: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: עַד שֶׁתִּפְרַח בְּכוּלּוֹ, אוֹ עַד שֶׁתִּמְעַט בַּהַרְתּוֹ מִכִּגְרִיס!

b3.he: רַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַויְיהוּ: כִּי קָנֵיס רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּמָמוֹנוֹ, בְּגוּפוֹ לָא קָנֵיס.

b4.he: מָמוֹנוֹ — אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּאָתֵי לְמֶיעְבַּד, גּוּפוֹ — מִי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּאָתֵי לְמֶיעְבַּד?

b5.he: אָמַר רָבָא: דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אַדְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר קַשְׁיָא, דְּרַבָּנַן אַדְּרַבָּנַן לָא קַשְׁיָא?

b6.he: אֶלָּא, דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אַדְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר לָא קַשְׁיָא, כִּדְשַׁנִּינַן. רַבָּנַן אַדְּרַבָּנַן נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָכָא בְּמַאי דַּעֲבַד קַנְסוּהּ, הָכָא בְּמַאי דַּעֲבַד קַנְסוּהּ.

b7.he: בְּמַאי אִיכַּוֵּין לְמִישְׁרְיֵיהּ בְּהַאי מוּמָא? בְּהַאי מוּמָא קַנְסוּהּ רַבָּנַן, דִּבְהַאי מוּמָא לָא לִישְׁתְּרֵי לֵיהּ. וְהָכָא, בְּמַאי דַּעֲבַד קַנְסוּהּ — אִיכַּוֵּין לְטַהוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּהַאי קְצִיצָה, בְּהַאי קְצִיצָה קַנְסוּהּ רַבָּנַן.

b8.he: בָּעֵי רַב פָּפָּא: ״יִטְהַר״ תְּנַן, אוֹ ״וְיִטְהָר״ תְּנַן?

b9.he: לְמַאי נָפְקָא מִינַּהּ? לְחָתָן שֶׁנִּרְאָה בּוֹ נֶגַע.

b10.he: דִּתְנַן: חָתָן שֶׁנִּרְאָה בּוֹ נֶגַע — נוֹתְנִין לוֹ שִׁבְעָה יָמִים, לוֹ וּלְאִצְטְלִיתוֹ וְלִכְסוּתוֹ, וְכֵן בָּרֶגֶל — נוֹתְנִין לוֹ כׇּל יְמֵי הָרֶגֶל.

b11.he: אִי אָמְרַתְּ ״יִטְהַר״ תְּנַן — מִקַּמַּיְיתָא טְהַר לֵיהּ, לְבָתְרָיְיתָא נָטְרִין לֵיהּ שִׁבְעָה יְמֵי מִשְׁתֶּה.

b12.he: אֶלָּא אִי אָמְרַתְּ: ״וְיִטְהַר״ תְּנַן — סוֹף סוֹף, כִּי לָא מְטַמֵּית לְבָתְרָיְיתָא, הָא מִיטַּמֵּא וְקָאֵי מִקַּמַּיְיתָא. מַאי? תֵּיקוּ.

b13.he: בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מֵרַבִּי זֵירָא: צוֹרֵם אוֹזֶן בַּבְּכוֹר וָמֵת, מַהוּ לִקְנוֹס בְּנוֹ אַחֲרָיו?

b14.he: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר: מוֹכֵר עַבְדּוֹ לַגּוֹיִם וָמֵת — קָנְסוּ בְּנוֹ אַחֲרָיו, דְּכֹל יוֹמָא וְיוֹמָא מַפְקַע לֵיהּ מִמִּצְוֹת.

b15.he: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר: כִּוֵּון מְלַאכְתּוֹ בַּמּוֹעֵד וָמֵת — לֹא קָנְסוּ בְּנוֹ אַחֲרָיו, מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא עַבְדֵהּ לְאִיסּוּרָא.

b16.he: הָכָא מַאי? לְדִידֵיהּ קְנַסוּ רַבָּנַן, וְהָא לֵיתֵיהּ, אוֹ דִלְמָא לְמָמוֹנֵיהּ קְנַסוּ רַבָּנַן, וְהָא אִיתֵיהּ?

b17.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תְּנֵיתוּהָ, שָׂדֶה שֶׁנִּתְקַוְּוצָה בִּשְׁבִיעִית — תִּזָּרַע לְמוֹצָאֵי שְׁבִיעִית, נִיטַּיְּיבָה נִידַּיְּירָה — לֹא תִּזָּרַע לְמוֹצָאֵי שְׁבִיעִית. וְאָמַר רַב אַסִּי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: נָקְטִינַן, הֱטִיבָהּ וָמֵת — בְּנוֹ זוֹרְעָהּ. אַלְמָא לְדִידֵיהּ קְנַסוּ רַבָּנַן, לִבְרֵיהּ לָא קְנַסוּ רַבָּנַן.

messages.text: Continued from 33b: the Gemara explained that the Rabbis use “There shall not be any blemish in it” to forbid causing a blemish even indirectly, as a baraita teaches: “There shall not be any blemish in it”; from here I have derived…
Gemara

…only the prohibition that one may not directly cause a blemish. From where is it derived that one may not bring pressed figs or dough and place it on the animal’s ear so that a dog will come and eat it, thereby biting off part of the animal’s ear and leaving it blemished?

The verse states: “There shall not be any blemish in it” (Leviticus 22:21), indicating that the same prohibition applies both when the blemish is caused directly and when it is any blemish, even one caused indirectly.

verse.he: וְאִישׁ כִּי־יַקְרִיב זֶבַח־שְׁלָמִים לַיהֹוָה לְפַלֵּא־נֶדֶר אוֹ לִנְדָבָה בַּבָּקָר אוֹ בַצֹּאן תָּמִים יִהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן כׇּל־מוּם לֹא יִהְיֶה־בּוֹ׃
verse.en: And when anyone offers, from the herd or the flock, a sacrifice of well-being to GOD for an explicit uncertain. vow or as a freewill offering, it must, to be acceptable, be without blemish; there must be no defect in it.

notes.he: ואפי' הני תנאי דלא דרשי כל בפרק אלו עוברין (פסחים מג:) אפשר דהכא דרשי שיש ענין כדפי' התם:
notes.en: Both a blemish and any blemish: even those tanna’im who do not expound “any [kol]”, in the chapter Elu Overin (Pesaḥim 43b), may expound it here, since there is a reason for it, as explained there.

notes.he: אמר מום דבידים ואמר כל מום שלא יגרום:
notes.en: It says “blemish”, for one caused by direct action, and it says “any blemish”, that he should not cause one [indirectly].

messages.text: It is stated in a verse addressed to Aaron and his sons: “And I, behold, I have given you the charge of My terumot [terumotai]” (Numbers 18:8), with “terumotai” written in plural.

verse.he: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל־אַהֲרֹן וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֶת־מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמֹתָי לְכׇל־קׇדְשֵׁי בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְךָ נְתַתִּים לְמׇשְׁחָה וּלְבָנֶיךָ לְחׇק־עוֹלָם׃
verse.en: GOD spoke further to Aaron: I hereby give you charge of My gifts, all the sacred donations of the Israelites; I grant them to you and to your sons as a perquisite, a due for all time.

messages.text: Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the barrel of teruma must be safeguarded from ritual impurity, holds that the verse is speaking of two terumot: Both teruma that is definitely ritually pure and teruma that is in abeyance, i.e., teruma whose status with regard to impurity is uncertain. And based on the plural “My terumot,” it is understood that the Merciful One states: Make a protection for it, i.e., safeguard even teruma whose status concerning impurity is uncertain.

notes.he: דכתיב משמרת:
notes.en: Make a protection for it: as it is written, “the charge [mishmeret]”.

notes.dh: אחת תרומה טהורה ואחת תרומה תלויה
notes.he: וא"ת דבפ' במה מדליקין (שבת כה. ושם) אמרי' ואחת טמאה ואמר רחמנא שלך תהא להסקה תחת תבשילך והיכי נפקי מקרא שלש תרומות טהורה וטמאה ותלויה וי"ל משום דכתיב נתתי לך משמרת תרומתי דקאי תרומתי אלך ואמשמרת דלך שייך אטמאה לרבוייה להיתר הנאה ומשמרת שייך בתלויה דבעיא שימור:
notes.en: One teruma that is pure and one teruma that is in abeyance: And if you say: in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (Shabbat 25a) we say “and one that is impure, and the Merciful One said: it shall be yours, for kindling under your cooked dish.” How, then, do three terumot emerge from the verse: pure, impure and in abeyance? One can say: since it is written “I have given you the charge of My terumot,” “My terumot” relates both to “you” and to “charge.” “You” relates to the impure teruma, to include it as permitted for benefit, and “charge” relates to the teruma in abeyance, which requires safeguarding.

messages.text: And Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that one may expose to ritual impurity the teruma contents in the barrel, holds that the term terumotai is written so that it can be read as terumati, meaning: My teruma, in the singular. Therefore, the requirement to safeguard teruma applies only to that teruma whose status is definitely pure.

notes.he: וא"ת לר' יהושע כיון דלא איירי קרא בשתי תרומות מנליה דטמאה שריא בהנאה וי"ל דנפק משאר דרשות דהתם בפרק במה מדליקין (ג"ז שם) ממנו אי אתה מבעיר כו' או מלו ולא לאורו מכלל דבת אורו הוא:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehoshua: “terumati” is written: And if you say: according to Rabbi Yehoshua, since the verse does not speak of two terumot, from where does he know that impure teruma is permitted for benefit? One can say that he derives it from the other expositions there, in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (ibid.): “From it you may not kindle…”, or “…but not for its light,” which implies that it is [otherwise] fit for its light [the wording here is abbreviated in the text].

notes.he: ור"י סבר תרומתי כתיב כלומר דתרומה טהורה בעיא שימור ולא תלויה:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds “terumati” is written: that is, teruma that is pure requires safeguarding, but not teruma in abeyance.

messages.text: Is this to say that Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization of the Torah is authoritative, i.e., one derives halakhot based on the pronunciation of the words, although it diverges from the spelling?

notes.dh: דר' אליעזר סבר יש אם למקרא
notes.he: כדקרינן ליה תרומותי:
notes.en: That Rabbi Eliezer holds the vocalization is authoritative: as we read it, “terumotai.”

messages.text: And the Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita discussing a Hebrew maidservant’s return to her father’s house:

The verse states, with regard to her master: “He shall have no power to sell her to a foreign people, seeing that he has dealt deceitfully with her [bevigdo bah]” (Exodus 21:8). The term “bevigdo” shares a root with a word for garment, beged. Therefore, the verse indicates that once the master has spread his garment over her, thereby designating her as his wife, if the maidservant is subsequently divorced or widowed, her father may no longer sell her. This is the statement of Rabbi Akiva, who maintains that the vocalization of the Torah is authoritative, and he interprets bevigdo as related to bigdo, his garment.

verse.he: אִם־רָעָה בְּעֵינֵי אֲדֹנֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר־[לוֹ] (לא) יְעָדָהּ וְהֶפְדָּהּ לְעַם נׇכְרִי לֹא־יִמְשֹׁל לְמׇכְרָהּ בְּבִגְדוֹ־בָהּ׃
verse.en: If she proves to be displeasing to her master, who designated her for himself, he must let her be redeemed; he shall not have the right to sell her to outsiders, since he broke faith with her.

notes.he: שיעדה אדון לאמה העבריה ונשאה ופירש כנפיו עליה שוב אין האב רשאי למוכרה אפי' גירשה אדון דאין אדם מוכר בתו לשפחות אחר אישות וקיימא לן בפ"ק דקדושין (דף יח:) דר"א סבר יש אם למסורת בבגדו בה כתיב בלא יו"ד וזהו לשון בגידה כשאר תיבות הכתובות בלא יו"ד שאתה קוראן חטף קמץ כמו (בראשית לט) כשמעו:
notes.en: Once he spread his garment over her: that the master designated the Hebrew maidservant [as his wife], married her and spread his wings over her. The father may no longer sell her, even if the master divorced her, since a man does not sell his daughter into servitude after marriage. And we have established in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18b) that Rabbi Eliezer holds that the spelling is authoritative: “bevigdo bah” is written without a yod, and that is the language of deceit [begida], like other words written without a yod that you read with a ḥataf kamatz, as in “kishmo’o” (Genesis 39).

notes.he: פי' בקונטרס דגרס כיון שפירש טליתו עליה שוב אינו רשאי למוכרה דברי ר"ע ר"א אומר כיון שבגד בה כו' ובפ"ק דקדושין (דף יח:) הביא ראי' מן המכילתא דגרס בדברי ר"ע כיון שפירש טליתו ודר' אליעזר ליתא התם וברוב ספרים ישנים גרסינן איפכא כאן ובקדושין (ג"ז שם) ועוד דלגירסת הקונטרס מקדים דברי ר"ע לדברי ר"א שהיה רבו ועוד כתוב ברוב ספרים בבגדו בה בבגדו בה תרי זימני כיון שפירש טליתו ועוד היכי משמע ליה לר"א המסורת לשון בגידה משום דכתיב בבגדו בלא יו"ד ה"נ לא כתיב בוי"ו ואע"ג דבלא וי"ו אתה קורא חטף קמץ כדפירש בקונטרס כשמעו כשמעם (בראשית לד) באמרם (אסתר ז) כעברם (מלכים ב ב) ה"נ כי הוי לשון בגד וטלית אין רגילות לכתוב יו"ד באמצע של פעולה ועוד בההיא שמעתין בקדושין בסמוך כתוב בכל הספרים ישנים ולר"נ בר יצחק דאמר מעות הראשונות לקדושין נתנו במאי מוקים לה כר"ע דאמר לשפחות אחר שפחות הוא דלא מצי למזבן אבל לשפחות אחר אישות מצי מיזבן ליה ולפי' הקונטרס צריך להגיה ר"א ונראה לר"ת דגרסינן כיון שפירש טליתו כו' דברי ר"א ר' עקיבא אומר כיון שבגד והשתא הוי לשון בגידה דאי לשון בגד וטלית הוי לן למקרי בבגדו בצירי ואע"ג דקרינן ותתפשהו בבגדו (בראשית ל״ט:י״ב) דשאני הכא דאיכא למיטעי והמסורת משמע טפי לשון בגד וטלית מלשון בגידה מדכתיב בבגדו בלא יו"ד ולכך אומר הברייתא תרי זימני בבגדו כיון שפירש טליתו כו' היה לך לכתוב בביגדו ביו"ד דלא ליתי למיטעי וכתיב בבגדו בלא יו"ד לומר כיון שפירש כו' ובמכילתא שגורס שפירש טליתו דברי ר"ע הסופר חיסר ודילג ר"א וגם כל מילתיה דר"ע ובדר"נ בר יצחק גרסינן מוקי לה כר"ע כמו שכתוב בכל הספרים ישנים וקצת קשיא הא דפריך התם בקדושין אלא דקידשה אביה מי מצי מזבין לה והא אין אדם מוכר בתו לשפחות אחר אישות בהך קושיא אליביה דר"א דשמותי הוא וי"ל דפשיטא לן שכן הלכה משום דרבנן דר"ש ור"ש גופיה דהתם דקיימי כוותיה ואמרי אבל לא לשפחות אחר אישות:
notes.en: In brief: Rashi’s text reads “once he spread his garment over her, he may no longer sell her” as the statement of Rabbi Akiva, and “since he dealt deceitfully with her” as Rabbi Eliezer’s, and in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18b) Rashi brings proof from the Mekhilta, which has “once he spread his garment” in Rabbi Akiva’s words and does not have Rabbi Eliezer’s at all. But most old manuscripts read the reverse, here and in Kiddushin (ibid.). Further: Rashi’s reading puts Rabbi Akiva’s words before those of Rabbi Eliezer, who was his teacher; most texts repeat “bevigdo bah, bevigdo bah” twice before “once he spread his garment”; and how would Rabbi Eliezer get “deceit” from the spelling without a yod, when it is not written with a vav either? Though without a vav one reads a ḥataf kamatz, as Rashi explained (kishmo’o, kishmo’am, be’omram, ke’ovram), so too, if it meant garment, one would not ordinarily write a yod in the middle of such a form. Also, in the nearby passage in Kiddushin all the old texts read that Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, who says the first money was given for betrothal, establishes it according to Rabbi Akiva, who says one cannot sell her into servitude after servitude but can after marriage; on Rashi’s reading one would have to emend this to Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbeinu Tam therefore reads: “Once he spread his garment over her…”: the statement of Rabbi Eliezer; Rabbi Akiva says: “Once he dealt deceitfully with her.” Then it is the vocalization that means deceit, for if it meant garment we would read “bevigdo” with a tzeirei (and although we read “vatitpesehu bevigdo,” Genesis 39:12, here is different, because one might err); and the spelling without a yod suggests garment more than deceit. That is why the baraita says “bevigdo” twice: you should have written it with a yod so as not to err, yet it is written without a yod to say “once he spread his garment…”. In the Mekhilta that has “spread his garment” in Rabbi Akiva’s words, the scribe left out Rabbi Eliezer and all of Rabbi Akiva’s own statement; and in Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak’s passage one reads “establishes it according to Rabbi Akiva,” as all the old texts have it. A slight difficulty remains: in Kiddushin the Gemara asks, “But if her father betrothed her, can he sell her? A man does not sell his daughter into servitude after marriage,” even though, on this reading, that is the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who is a Shammaite. One can say it is obvious to us that this is the halakha, because the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon there, and Rabbi Shimon himself, agree with him and say: but not into servitude after marriage. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

notes.he: כיון שפרש טליתו עליה לשום יעוד שוב אינו רשאי למוכרה אלמא דאזיל אחר מסורת דפשטיה דקרא הוי לשון בגידה כלומר כיון שבגד בה שמכרה פעם אחת שוב אינו רשאי למכרה:
notes.en: And the Gemara raises a contradiction: “bevigdo bah.” [An editor’s footnote here says that Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading is like that of Tosafot, in the comment beginning “Ilema”.] Once he spread his garment over her for designation, he may no longer sell her. Evidently he follows the spelling, since the plain sense of the verse is the language of deceit, that is: since he dealt deceitfully with her by selling her once, he may no longer sell her.

messages.text: The word bevigdo is written without a yod and therefore is written in a manner that it can be read: Bevagdo. Accordingly, bevigdo bah means that since the father dealt deceitfully [bagad] with her by selling her once, he may not sell her again.

notes.he: אביה שמכרה לשפחות שוב אינו רשאי למוכרה דאין אדם מוכר את בתו לשפחות אחר שפחות אבל לאחר אישות מצי לזבונה ואמרי התם דר"ע סבר יש אם למקרא בבגדו קרינא. ויש שמשבשין השמועה במס' קדושין וגורסין ר"א סבר יש אם למקרא ור"ע סבר יש אם למסורת וטעות הוא בידם דא"כ מאי מקשי הכא בבכורות:
notes.en: Since he dealt deceitfully with her: her father, who sold her into servitude, may no longer sell her, since a man does not sell his daughter into servitude after servitude; but after marriage he may sell her. And they say there [in Kiddushin] that Rabbi Akiva holds that the vocalization is authoritative: we read “bevigdo” [his garment]. Some corrupt the passage in tractate Kiddushin and read: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization is authoritative and Rabbi Akiva holds that the spelling is authoritative. But they are in error, for if so, what is the difficulty raised here in Bekhorot?

notes.he: ור' אליעזר דריש בתר מסורת לשון בגד טלית דאי כפשטיה מיסתייה למימר בבגד בה מדכתיב בבגדו היינו בגד והא מילתא קשיא לההיא דגמרינן במסכת קדושין דהתם קאמר במאי קא מיפלגי ר' אליעזר סבר יש אם למקרא ס"א משמיה דר' יצחק האור' ז"ל כיון שבגד בה שוב אין לאביה רשות בה דברי ר' אליעזר אלמא קסבר יש אם למסורת למאי דכתיב בבגדו ולא כדקרינן בבגדו. וקשיא נמי להאי דקידושין דהתם אמר ר' אליעזר דכיון שפירש טליתו וקאמר יש אם למקרא אלא בלך פליגי ואני הנה נתתי לך:
notes.en: And Rabbi Eliezer expounds according to the spelling, as the language of a garment, a cloak; for if it were as its plain sense, it would have been enough to say “bevaged bah.” Since “bevigdo” is written, that is “garment.” And this is difficult for what we learn in tractate Kiddushin, where it says: “In what do they disagree? Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization is authoritative.” Another version, in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak the Elder, of blessed memory: “Once he dealt deceitfully with her, her father no longer has authority over her; the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.” Evidently he holds that the spelling is authoritative, according to what is written, “bevagdo,” and not as we read it, “bevigdo.” And it is also difficult for that passage in Kiddushin, where Rabbi Eliezer said “once he spread his cloak” and it says that the vocalization is authoritative. Rather, they disagree about “you”: “And I, behold, I have given you.” [The text of this comment is difficult; we have rendered it as it stands.]

messages.text: Tosafot, following Rabbeinu Tam, reads this baraita with the two opinions reversed: “spread his garment” as Rabbi Eliezer’s and “dealt deceitfully” as Rabbi Akiva’s; Rabbeinu Gershom also takes the “garment” exposition as Rabbi Eliezer’s. The chat follows the daf’s text and the Davidson English (see their notes).

Evidently, Rabbi Eliezer maintains that the manner in which the verses in the Torah are written is authoritative, and one derives halakhot based on the spelling of the words. This contradicts his derivation with regard to teruma, which is based on the pronunciation of the words.
messages.quote: since the father dealt deceitfully with her

messages.text: Rather, here, the tanna’im disagree with regard to this: The verse states: “And I, behold, I have given you the charge of My terumot” (Numbers 18:8).

Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the term “you” teaches that only teruma that is fit for you to eat, i.e., teruma that is definitely ritually pure, you must safeguard. But teruma that is not fit for you, i.e., teruma whose status with regard to impurity is uncertain, you do not need to safeguard.

notes.he: הראויה לך שהיא טהורה שמור:
notes.en: That which is fit for you: which is pure, safeguard.

messages.text: And Rabbi Eliezer holds that this teruma, whose status with regard to impurity is uncertain, is also considered fit for you, because perhaps Elijah will come and deem it ritually pure.
The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon.
messages.lead: § The Gemara again discusses letting the blood of a firstborn offering.

messages.text: To which opinion of Rabbi Shimon is Shmuel referring? If we say he is referring to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in the mishna, that the blood may be let despite the resulting blemish, because the purpose of the treatment is solely medical, that cannot be correct. After all, hasn’t Shmuel taught us until now that an unintentional act, i.e., a permitted action from which a prohibited result inadvertently ensues, is permitted?
messages.lead: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak objects to this:
messages.quote: in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon

notes.he: דאמר במתני' יקיז אע"פ (שיש בו) מום ולא קאמר דישחט עליו:
notes.en: Rabbi Shimon: who says in the mishna, “One may let the blood even though it causes a blemish,” and does not say that one may slaughter on account of it.

notes.dh: אילימא ר"ש דמתני' עד השתא לא אשמעינן שמואל דבר שאין מתכוין מותר
notes.he: תימה אטו מי שרי ר"ש משום דאין מתכוין הא אפי' במקום שא"א שלא יעשה מום נמי שרי דעושה מום במתכוין כדאמר לעיל דבקראי פליגי ושרי משום דכתיב (ויקרא כ״ב:כ״א) תמים יהיה לרצון אבל מטיל בבעל מום שרי ובפ' כל המנחות באות מצה (מנחות נו:) מפרש נמי טעמייהו מקראי ולפי' הקונ' דלעיל בפרק הלוקח בהמה (בכורות דף כה.) גבי שתי שערות של פרה שעיקרן מאדים וראשן משחיר וקאמר ר' יוסי בן המשולם גוזז במספרים ואינו חושש ופי' בקונט' דחשיב אין מתכוין משום דאין מתכוין לגיזה אלא לתקן את הפרה ניחא נמי הכא דאין מתכוין משום הטלת מום אלא משום רפואה ולהכי פריך אמאי איצטריך ליה לשמואל לפסוק כר"ש דאפי' הוה אסר מטיל מום בבעל מום הוי שרי הכא משום דאין אלא לרפואה ושמואל אית ליה דבר שאין מתכוין מותר ומיהו א"א לקיים פי' הקונ' כדפרישית לעיל בפ' הלוקח בהמה (ג"ז שם.) ונראה לפרש הכא דבתרתי פליגי דבברייתא פליגי במטיל מום בבעל מום שאחזו דם ביותר וא"א לו להתרפאות בלא הקזה שלא ימות כדאמר לעיל דאי שביק ליה מיית דאז חשיב מום ואפי' לא מיית נמי כיון שלעולם לא יצא מאחוזת דם אם לא יקיזנו במקום שעושה מום חשיב כבעל מום והשתא ר"מ אסר במקום שעושה מום דקסבר כו' לא יהיה בו אפי' בבעל מום וחכמים שרו משום דכתיב תמים יהיה לרצון ובלבד שלא ישחט על אותו מום דגזר אטו היכא דלא מיית בלא עשיית מום דחשיב כתם או אטו היכא דיכול להתרפאות בהקזה במקום שאין אתה עושה מום ור"ש שרי אף לשחוט דלא גזר ור' יהודה אסר אף במקום שאין עושה מום כדמפרש בפ"ק דפסחים (דף יא:) דמתוך שאדם בהול על ממונו אי שרית במקום שאין עושה מום אתי למיעבד במקום שעושה מום ובמתניתין היא פלוגתא אחרת דר' יהודה קאמר בכור שאחזו דם אפי' מת אין מקיזין בשום ענין כדפרישית וחכ"א יקיז פי' בין מת בין לא מת ובלבד שלא יעשה בו מום כלומר שיזהר בהקזתו שלא יוכל לבא לידי מום כשיקיז סמוך לאוזן או לניב שפתים או לחוטם דקסבר דבר שאין מתכוין אסור והיכא דלא מיית דלא חשיב בעל מום אסור ר"ש אומר יקיז אע"פ שהוא עושה מום שהוא יכול לבא לידי עשיית מום דדבר שאין מתכוין מותר ולשון המשנה משמע ליה כמו שפירשנו מדלא נקט מקום שעושה בו מום ומקום שאין עושה בו מום כדנקיט בברייתא וא"ת וכיון דאחוזת דם חשיב כמום שאין יכול להתרפאות בלא עשיית מום א"כ לשחוט עילויה וי"ל דמדרבנן אסור דאתי לאיחלופי בתם א"נ חשיב כמו [מום] עובר שיש לו רפואה:
notes.en: In brief: If we say it is Rabbi Shimon of the mishna, hasn’t Shmuel already taught us that an unintentional act is permitted? This is puzzling: does Rabbi Shimon permit because the act is unintentional? He permits even where it is impossible not to cause a blemish, which is causing a blemish intentionally, since it was said above that they disagree about verses, and he permits because it is written “It shall be perfect to be accepted” (Leviticus 22:21): one who causes a blemish in an already blemished animal is permitted; and in the chapter Kol HaMenaḥot Ba’ot Matza (Menaḥot 56b) their reasons are likewise explained from verses. On Rashi’s explanation earlier, in the chapter HaLoke’aḥ Behema (25a), of the two hairs of a cow whose roots are red and tips black, where Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says one may shear them with scissors without concern, Rashi explained that it counts as unintentional, since he intends not to shear but to fix the cow. On that view this passage works well too: here it is unintentional with regard to the blemish, being only for healing, so the Gemara asks why Shmuel needed to rule like Rabbi Shimon, since even if one prohibited causing a blemish in a blemished animal it would be permitted here as healing, and Shmuel already holds that an unintentional act is permitted. But Rashi’s explanation cannot stand, as explained there. Better to explain that there are two disputes. In the baraita they disagree about causing a blemish in an animal already blemished: one so congested with blood that it cannot be healed without bloodletting and would die, which counts as a blemish; and even if it would not die, since it would never be free of the congestion unless one let blood where it causes a blemish, it counts as blemished. Rabbi Meir prohibits letting blood where it causes a blemish, since he holds “there shall be no blemish in it” applies even to a blemished animal; the Rabbis permit, because of “It shall be perfect to be accepted,” but not slaughtering on account of that blemish, as a decree lest one do so where it would not die without a blemish, and counts as unblemished, or where it could be healed by letting blood where no blemish results; Rabbi Shimon permits even slaughtering, as he does not decree; and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits even where no blemish results, as explained in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (11b): since a person is anxious about his money, if you permit it where no blemish results he will come to do it where one does. In the mishna the dispute is different: Rabbi Yehuda says one may not let the blood in any way, even if it would die; the Rabbis say one may, whether or not it would die, provided one takes care not to cause a blemish, for example near the ear, the lips or the nose, since they hold that an unintentional act is prohibited, and where it would not die it does not count as blemished; Rabbi Shimon says one may let blood even though it may lead to a blemish, since an unintentional act is permitted. The wording of the mishna suggests this, since it does not speak of a place that causes a blemish and a place that does not, as the baraita does. And if you ask: since congestion that cannot be healed without a blemish counts as a blemish, let one slaughter on account of it? It is prohibited by rabbinic law, lest it be confused with an unblemished animal; or it counts as a passing blemish that has a cure. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

messages.text: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that an unintentional act is prohibited,
messages.lead: But doesn’t Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi say that Rav says:

notes.he: במס' שבת (דף כב.) דאמר דבר שאין מתכוין אסור:
notes.en: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: in tractate Shabbat (22a), who says that an unintentional act is prohibited.

messages.text: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, that an unintentional act is permitted.
messages.lead: and Rav Ḥanin bar Ashi says that Shmuel says:

notes.he: ולמה ליה תו לאשמועי' הכא:
notes.en: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: so why would he need to teach it again here?

messages.text: Rav says that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, and Shmuel says that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon.
messages.lead: And Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin teaches these rulings directly, without citing additional men in their transmission. He simply states that

notes.he: בלא רב חייא ורב חנן:
notes.en: Without men: without Rav Ḥiyya and Rav Ḥanan [Rashi writes “Rav Ḥanan”, where the Davidson English here has Rav Ḥanin bar Ashi].

messages.text: Evidently, Shmuel could not be referring to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in the mishna, as if so, he would be repeating himself.

Rather, Shmuel is referring to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in the baraita (33b), that not only may one let the blood of the dying firstborn animal despite the resulting blemish, but it is even permitted to eat the animal’s meat on account of the blemish.
messages.quote: To which opinion of Rabbi Shimon is Shmuel referring?

notes.he: דאמר אף ישחט על אותו המום כיון דלא היה דעתו להטיל בו מום כדי להתירו אלא כדי שלא ימות לא קנסינן ליה:
notes.en: Of the baraita: who says that one may even slaughter on account of that blemish. Since his intention was not to cause a blemish in order to permit it, but so that it would not die, we do not penalize him.

notes.he: דברייתא דאמר אף נשחט על אותו המום. טעמא דרבן גמליאל דאמר לא יחדש בה דבר היינו כר' אליעזר שמא יבא אליהו ויטהרם:
notes.en: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: of the baraita, who says one may even slaughter on account of that blemish. The reason of Rabban Gamliel, who said “one should do nothing new with it,” is like that of Rabbi Eliezer: lest Elijah come and deem them pure.

messages.text: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon as stated in the baraita.
messages.lead: And the Gemara notes that Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, teaches this explicitly: Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says:

messages.text: Mishna
In the case of one who slits [hatzorem] the ear of a firstborn offering, that person may never slaughter that animal. This is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.

notes.he: הפוגם אנקרני"ר בלע"ז. ובכהן קא מיירי:
notes.en: Mishna. One who slits: who damages it (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). And it is speaking of a priest.

notes.he: הפוגם במתכוין הרי זה לא ישחוט עולמית דקנסינן ליה:
notes.en: One who slits: who damages it intentionally may never slaughter it, since we penalize him.

messages.text: If another blemish later develops in the firstborn, he may slaughter the animal on account of that second blemish.

notes.he: לא ישחוט על זה אבל כשנולד בו מום אחר ישחט עליו:
notes.en: And the Rabbis say: he may not slaughter on account of this blemish, but when another blemish develops in it, he may slaughter on account of that one.

messages.text: Gemara
But does Rabbi Eliezer penalize for a transgression forever? And the Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna (Nega’im 7:5):
messages.quote: that person may never slaughter that animal

notes.he: שלעולם לא יהא מותר:
notes.en: Gemara. But does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever: that it will never be permitted?

notes.dh: ומי קניס ר"א לעולם ורמינהי מי שהיתה לו
notes.he: כמה שמעתתא מוכחא דצורם אוזן של בכור קנסא הוא ובסמוך נמי קאמר בהאי מומא קנסוה רבנן ואפי' לרבא דאמר בפ"ק דתמורה (דף ד:) מילתא דאמר רחמנא לא תעביד אי עביד לא מהני מכל מקום הכא שרי האי בכור מדאורייתא דהאי יש בו מום והאי גברא טהור דהא אין בו נגע כלל וא"ת דבספרי בפרשה ראה אנכי תניא רבי אליעזר אומר כו' המטיל מום בבכור ואוכלו עובר שנאמר לא תאכל כל תועבה אלמא דמדאורייתא אסור (וי"ל) דבסמוך אשכחן ליה קנסא לרבנן דסברי כאחרים דדרשי התם בפסולי המוקדשין הכתוב מדבר או בבישול בשר בחלב כדקאמר בפ' כל הבשר (חולין קיד:) ואין לאסור שחיטה על אותו מום מלא תאכל כל תועבה כמו בשר בחלב וכלאי זרעים ומעשה שבת שיש לחלק וא"ת ולר"א דלא מפליג מאי פריך עליה מבהרת דגבי צורם אוזן בבכור דאסור מדאורייתא עד שיולד מום אחר יש לנו לקנסו כשנולד בו מום אבל קוצץ בהרת דמדאורייתא טהור מיד שנקצץ עד שיוולד נגע אחר וי"ל דאפ"ה לא היה לנו לקנוס במום עולמית אלא עד מום שלישי או רביעי א"נ נהי דאי יתיר ר"א לשחוט במום אחר אין כאן קנס מ"מ לא היה לנו לקנוס במום שלא עשה בו עבירה כי היכי דלא קניס בנגע אחר א"נ דספרי אסמכתא בעלמא הוא:
notes.en: But does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever? And the Gemara raises a contradiction: one who had…: Several passages prove that the ruling on one who slits the ear of a firstborn is a penalty, and just below too it says: “with this blemish the Rabbis penalized him.” And even according to Rava, who says in the first chapter of Temura (4b) that whatever the Merciful One said not to do, if one does it, it is ineffective, here the firstborn is permitted by Torah law, since it has a blemish, and this man is pure, since he has no leprous mark at all. And if you say: in the Sifrei, on the portion Re’eh, it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer says… one who causes a blemish in a firstborn and eats it transgresses, as it is said: “You shall not eat any abomination” (Deuteronomy 14:3); evidently it is prohibited by Torah law? One can say: just below we find this penalty according to the Rabbis, who hold like the Aḥerim, who expound that verse there as speaking of disqualified consecrated animals or of cooking meat in milk, as stated in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 114b); and one cannot prohibit slaughtering on account of that blemish from “You shall not eat any abomination,” as with meat in milk, diverse kinds of seeds and work done on Shabbat, for one can distinguish. And if you say: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who does not make that distinction, what is the challenge from the baheret? One who slits the ear of a firstborn is prohibited by Torah law until another blemish develops, so we should penalize him when another blemish develops; whereas one who excises a baheret is pure by Torah law as soon as it is excised, [and is penalized only] until another mark develops. One can say: even so, we should not have penalized him forever with the blemish, but only until a third or fourth blemish. Alternatively: granted that if Rabbi Eliezer permitted slaughter for another blemish there would be no penalty here at all, still we should not penalize him with a blemish through which he committed no transgression, just as he does not penalize him with another leprous mark. Alternatively, the Sifrei is a mere supporting allusion [asmakhta].

messages.text: In the case of one who had a snow-white leprous mark [baheret] on his body,

and it inadvertently got excised, that individual is ritually pure. If he excised it intentionally, in an attempt to render himself ritually pure, the Sages impose a punitive impurity upon him. The tanna’im disagree with regard to the extent of the penalty:

notes.he: שלא נתכוין לקצצה:
notes.en: And it got excised: he did not intend to excise it.

notes.he: מעצמה:
notes.en: And it got excised: by itself.

messages.text: When he will develop another leprous mark, his status of ritual purity is assessed based on this new mark. When that mark is ruled ritually pure, he will become ritually pure from the ritual impurity generated by the mark he excised.

notes.he: שהרי הוא עכשיו טמא ומנוגע:
notes.en: When he will develop another leprous mark: for now he is impure and afflicted [by this new mark].

notes.he: מן הראשונה והולכין אחר זו ואם ירפא מזו טהור מכולם דאיגלאי מילתא דאי (נמי) הוי קמייתא מיתסי נמי כי האי:
notes.en: He will become pure: from the first one. We follow this one, and if he is healed of it, he is pure of them all, since it has become clear that the first one too would have healed like this one.

messages.text: The development of a new leprous mark is insufficient. Rather, he must wait either until the leprosy of the new mark spreads over his entire body, a sign of ritual purity (see Leviticus 13:12), or unless his old baheret had shrunk to a size smaller than that of a split bean before he excised it. Otherwise, he remains ritually impure.

verse.he: וְאִם־פָּרוֹחַ תִּפְרַח הַצָּרַעַת בָּעוֹר וְכִסְּתָה הַצָּרַעַת אֵת כׇּל־עוֹר הַנֶּגַע מֵרֹאשׁוֹ וְעַד־רַגְלָיו לְכׇל־מַרְאֵה עֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן׃
verse.en: If the eruption spreads out over the skin so that it covers all the skin of the affected person from head to foot, wherever the priest can see—

notes.he: נגע האחרון וליכא למיחש למידי דהא אי הוה ביה קמא השתא נמי הוה טהור כדכתיב (ויקרא י״ג:י״ב) וכסתה הצרעת את כל עור הנגע וגו':
notes.en: Until it spreads over all of him: the latter mark. Then there is nothing to be concerned about, since even if the first mark were on him it would now be pure, as it is written: “And if the leprosy cover all the skin of him that has the plague” (Leviticus 13:12).

notes.he: הראשונה מכגריס קודם שקצצה אבל אי בשעה שקצצה הוה ביה שיעור נגע אין לו טהרה עולמית דקנסינן ליה לעולם:
notes.en: Or until his baheret shrinks: the first one, to less than a split bean, before he excised it. But if at the time he excised it, it was the size of a leprous mark, he has no purification ever, since we penalize him forever.

notes.he: בכל הספרים [כתוב] עד שתתמעט בהרתו מכגריס אבל במס' נגעים ליתיה כדפי' בקונט' ואומר רבי דאי גרסינן לי' ה"פ שאם קצצה ונעשה בכגריס ומה ששייר נתרפא מקצתו מעצמו שאפי' היה בו מה שנקצצה לא היה בו כגריס:
notes.en: Until it spreads over all of him: in all the texts it is written “or until his baheret shrinks to less than a split bean,” but in tractate Nega’im it is not there, as Rashi explained. And my teacher says that if we do read it, this is the meaning: he excised it and it became exactly a split bean, and of what remained part healed by itself, so that even if the part he excised were still there it would not be the size of a split bean.

notes.he: לעולם לא יטהר עד שתפרח בכולו בכל גופו הנגע השני דהשתא הוי טהור מדאורייתא דכתיב וכסתה הצרעת מראשו ועד רגליו וגו':
notes.en: And the Rabbis say: he will never become pure until the second mark spreads over all of him, over his whole body, for then he is pure by Torah law, as it is written: “And if the leprosy… cover… from his head even to his feet” (Leviticus 13:12).

messages.text: In any event, it is clear from this mishna that Rabbi Eliezer does not impose an indefinite penalty on one who transgresses. If so, why does he impose an indefinite penalty in the mishna discussing one who causes a blemish on the ear of a firstborn offering?

notes.he: כלומר דההוא נגע ראשון דקציץ במתכוין אי לא הוה ביה כגריס דהיינו שיעור דאורייתא טהור מיד ואי הוה ביה כגריס לא יטהר עד שיולד בו נגע אחר ויפרח בכולו ור' אליעזר סבר אע"ג דהוא דקציץ הוה כגריס כיון שנולד בו מום אחר וטהר ממני טהר נמי מן הראשון. ולא בעי עד שתפרח בכולו אלמא דלא קניס ר' אליעזר הכא ורבנן קנסי:
notes.en: Or until his baheret shrinks to less than a split bean: that is, if that first mark, which he excised intentionally, was not the size of a split bean, which is the Torah measure, he is pure immediately; and if it was the size of a split bean, he will not become pure until another mark develops in him and spreads over all of him. And Rabbi Eliezer holds that even though the one he excised was the size of a split bean, once another mark develops in him and he becomes pure of it, he becomes pure of the first as well, and it need not spread over all of him. Evidently Rabbi Eliezer does not penalize here, and the Rabbis do.

messages.text: When Rabbi Eliezer penalizes one who transgresses, that is only in a case which involves his property, e.g., a firstborn offering. But in a case which affects his body, e.g., leprosy, he does not penalize him to such an extent.

With regard to his property, i.e., the firstborn offering, if he would not be penalized indefinitely, there is reason to say that he might come to perform an action which would cause a blemish. Since the firstborn offering is anyway prohibited for personal use until it is blemished, he suffers no risk in blemishing it. A greater deterrent than usual is therefore needed to prevent such action.

notes.he: ממה נפשך דסבר אטיל בו מום ואם יתירוהו לי בכך הרי נשכרתי ואם לאו מה הפסדתי אם אמתין למום אחר בלא"ה נמי הייתי ממתין עד שיפול מום הלכך קנסינן ליה אפי' יפול בו מום אחר כי היכי דלא ליתי וליעביד:
notes.en: With his property he might come to do it: either way. He thinks: I will cause a blemish in it, and if they permit it to me on account of this, I have gained; and if not, what have I lost? If I wait for another blemish, I would have waited for a blemish to develop anyway. Therefore we penalize him even if another blemish develops in it, so that he will not come to do it.

notes.he: בבכור קניס דאיכא למימר דאתי למעבד ביה מום ממה נפשך דסבר אי שרו ליה בההיא מומא שפיר ואי לא שרו ליה סבר השתא לא גריע כקודם לכן. דקודם לכן הוה אסורי למיכל והשתא נמי אסור גופו מי איכא למימר דאתי למעבד לקוץ לכתחלה ממה נפשך דמאי ממה נפשך איכא הכא אי קציץ ליה שמא יולד לו נגע אחר וכשיטהר ממנו יטהר גם מזה מוטב לו שלא יקוץ זה וימתין עד שיטהר מזה ויהיה טהור משיקצצנו וימתין עד שיולד לו אחר הלכך לא קניס ר' אליעזר הכא דלא אתי למעבד איניש אחרינא לקוץ לכתחלה אבל בממונו בבכור קניס:
notes.en: With his property: with a firstborn he penalizes, since there is reason to say that he might come to cause a blemish in it either way. He thinks: if they permit it to me on account of that blemish, good; and if they do not, he thinks it is now no worse than before, since before it was forbidden to eat and now too it is forbidden. With his body, is there reason to say that he would come to excise it in the first place, either way? What “either way” is there here? If he excises it, perhaps another mark will develop, and when he becomes pure of it he will become pure of this one too; better for him not to excise this one and to wait until he becomes pure of it [by itself], than that he excise it and wait until another develops. Therefore Rabbi Eliezer does not penalize here, since another person would not come to excise it in the first place; but with his property, a firstborn, he penalizes.

messages.text: By contrast, in the case of leprosy on his body, is there a basis to say that he will come to perform an action and remove the white spot? In this case, the limited penalty of having to wait for purification from another leprous mark serves as a sufficient deterrent, as there is no guarantee that another mark will ever appear.

notes.he: דמנחי' לספיקא וליקוץ אי לא קנסינן ליה לעולם הא ודאי לא עביד דחייש שמא נגע אחר לא יוולד לו לעולם ולא אטהר לעולם ואפי' אם יוולד מה אהני לו בקציצה הרי הוא נגוע כבתחלה מוטב לו להניח את זה שמא ירפא:
notes.en: With his body, is there reason to say: that he would leave the doubt as it is and excise it, if we did not penalize him forever? He certainly will not do so, because he is concerned that another mark may never develop, and he will never become pure. And even if one does develop, what did the excision help him? He is afflicted as at first. Better for him to leave this one, and perhaps it will heal.

messages.text: Is this to say that the statement of Rabbi Eliezer in the mishna here is difficult in light of the other statement of Rabbi Eliezer in the mishna in Nega’im, whereas the statement of the Rabbis in the mishna is not difficult in light of the other statement of the Rabbis in Nega’im? In the mishna here, the Rabbis impose a limited penalty on the transgressor, whereas in the mishna in Nega’im they impose an indefinite one. This contradiction also requires resolution.

Rather, say: The statement of Rabbi Eliezer in the mishna here is not difficult in light of the statement of Rabbi Eliezer in Nega’im, as we answered. Likewise, the statement of the Rabbis in the mishna is not difficult in light of the statement of the Rabbis in Nega’im, as both rulings follow the same logic. Here, the Rabbis penalized him for what he did, and there, the Rabbis penalized him for what he did.

notes.he: דהכא במאי דעבד קנסוה דנתכוון למשרייה בהאי מומא קנסוה רבנן דחשבינן לההוא מום כמאן דליתיה אבל כשיולד בו מום אחר ישחט עליו. והכא במאי דעבד קנסוה דנתכוון לקצוץ ליטהר עצמו קנסוה רבנן דהוי כמאן דלא איקצץ דאפילו כשטהר מנגע שני חשבינן ליה לראשון דאכתי קאי ומשום הכי לא טהר עד שתפרח בכולו:
notes.en: The Rabbis are not difficult in light of the Rabbis: for here they penalized him with what he did: he intended to permit it with this blemish, so the Rabbis penalized him by treating that blemish as though it were not there; but when another blemish develops in it, he may slaughter on account of that. And there they penalized him with what he did: he intended to excise it in order to purify himself, so the Rabbis penalized him, and it is as though it had not been excised; even when he becomes pure of the second mark we treat the first as though it were still there, and for that reason he does not become pure until it spreads over all of him.

messages.text: In the case of causing a blemish in a firstborn offering, by what means did he intend to permit it? By means of this blemish. Therefore, the Rabbis penalized him only with regard to this blemish, i.e., that the animal will not become permitted to him by means of this blemish that he himself caused. The firstborn offering retains its status as unblemished and will become permitted only if it develops another blemish.

notes.he: לא מישתרי ליה עד שיוולד לו אחר:
notes.en: With this blemish: it will not be permitted to him until another one develops in it.

messages.text: And similarly, here, with regard to the removal of the leprous mark, the Rabbis penalize him for what he did. He intended to render himself ritually pure by means of this act of excising the mark. Therefore, the Rabbis penalized him with regard to this act of excision. It is considered as though he did not excise the mark, and as a result, he remains impure permanently.

notes.he: וכיון דהך קציצה אינה מועלת לטהרו נמצא טמא עולמית דחשבינן לנגע כמאן דאיתיה דמי יימר דאי הוה ביה הוה מיתסי:
notes.en: With this excision: since this excision does not help to purify him, he turns out to be impure forever, because we treat the mark as though it were still there. Who is to say that, had it been there, it would have healed?

messages.caption: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis on the two deliberate acts, with the Gemara’s two resolutions.

messages.text: What is the correct version of Rabbi Eliezer’s statement? Did we learn: Yit’har, or did we learn: Veyit’har, and he will become ritually pure?
messages.lead: § The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Eliezer’s statement: When he will develop another leprous mark, he will become ritually pure [yit’har] from the first. Rav Pappa asks:
messages.quote: When he will develop another leprous mark, he will become ritually pure from

notes.he: לכשיולד לו נגע אחר יטהר או ויטהר תנן יטהר משמע דכשנולד לו נגע אחר וירפא יטהר למפרע מן הראשון משעת קציצה או ויטהר תנן דמשמע דהשתא כשנרפא מן הנגע השני הוא דטהר ליה מן הראשון ולא למפרע משעת קציצה:
notes.en: Did we learn yit’har: “When he will develop another leprous mark, he will become pure”; or did we learn veyit’har? Yit’har implies that when another mark develops in him and is healed, he becomes pure retroactively of the first, from the time of the excision; or did we learn veyit’har, which implies that only now, when he is healed of the second mark, does he become pure of the first, and not retroactively from the time of the excision.

messages.text: Yit’har indicates that he will immediately be rendered ritually pure from the first leprous mark upon the appearance of the second mark. Veyit’har, by contrast, indicates that the punitive ritual impurity by rabbinic law imparted by the first mark remains until the second mark is deemed ritually pure.

notes.he: דמשמע מיד כשיוולד בו נגע אחר יטהר מן הראשונה:
notes.en: Did we learn yit’har: which implies that as soon as another mark develops in him, he becomes pure of the first.

notes.he: דמשמע כשיוולד נגע אחר ויטהר ממנו מן האחרון אז יטהר מן הראשון:
notes.en: Or did we learn veyit’har: which implies that when another mark develops and he becomes pure of it, of the latter one, then he becomes pure of the first.

messages.text: What is the practical difference between the two versions? After all, he is in any case ritually impure due to the second mark until that mark is deemed pure.
messages.quote: Did we learn: Yit’har, or did we learn: Veyit’har

notes.he: הא א"נ יטהר תנן הא טמא הוא מן האחרון עד שתרפא (ממה נפשך) וממה נפשך טומאה שייכא ביה:
notes.en: What is the practical difference: even if we learned yit’har, he is impure because of the latter one until it heals; either way, impurity applies to him.

messages.text: There is a difference in the case of a bridegroom who had removed a leprous mark upon whom a new leprous mark appeared during the seven days of his wedding celebrations.

notes.he: דנגע האחרון נולד לו בימי חתנות:
notes.en: For a bridegroom upon whom a leprous mark appeared: that the latter mark developed in him during the days of his wedding.

notes.he: מ"מ בין כך ובין כך לא יטהר עד שירפא מן השני נפקא מינה לחתן שנולד לו נגע אחר ביום חתונתו כלומר שכשנולד לו הנגע האחר היה חתן ולחתן שנולד לו נגע נותנין לו ז' ימי משתה ולא מטמינן ליה בין שנולד בו נגע ובין שנולד באיצטליתו או בכסותו דלא מצערינן ליה כל ימי חתונתו ולא כל ימי הרגל:
notes.en: What is the practical difference: either way he will not become pure until he is healed of the second. The difference is for a bridegroom in whom another mark developed on his wedding day, that is, when the other mark developed he was a bridegroom; and to a bridegroom in whom a mark developed they grant the seven days of feasting and do not declare him impure, whether it developed on him or on his cloak or his garment, since we do not distress him all the days of his wedding, nor all the days of the Festival.

messages.text: In the case of a bridegroom upon whom a leprous mark appeared, the court grants him seven days of his wedding celebrations before the mark is examined by a priest. This grace period is granted to him whether the mark appeared on him, i.e., his body, or on his cloak, or on any other garment of his.

notes.he: שלא יראה כהן את הנגע דכל כמה דלא חזי ליה כהן ולא מטמא ליה לא הוי טמא דבכהן תלא רחמנא:
notes.en: They grant him: that the priest will not examine the mark, since as long as the priest has not seen it and declared him impure, he is not impure, for the Merciful One made it depend on the priest.

notes.he: טליתו אם נולדו בה נגעי בגדים:
notes.en: For his cloak: his garment, if marks of garments developed in it.

messages.text: And similarly, with regard to any individual upon whom a leprous mark appeared during a pilgrimage Festival, the court grants him all the days of the pilgrimage Festival as a grace period, during which the mark is not examined by a priest.

If you say that we learned that the correct reading of Rabbi Eliezer’s statement is yit’har, i.e., the individual is rendered ritually pure upon the development of the new mark, this means that he is ritually pure during the seven-day period, as he has already become ritually pure of the punitive impurity from the first mark. As for the latter mark, we wait the seven days of feasting for him, before the mark is examined by a priest. He is therefore ritually pure in all regards.

notes.he: מיד כשנולד זה ומזה אינו טמא דנטרינן ליה יומי דחתונה או של רגל לכל אדם. אלא אי ויטהר תנן סוף סוף לא מהני ליה מידי הא דנטרינן ליה דאינו טהור מראשונה עד שתתרפא אחרונה:
notes.en: From the first he has become pure: as soon as this one developed, and of this one he is not impure, since we wait for him the days of the wedding, or of the Festival for anyone. But if we learned veyit’har, ultimately our waiting for him does not help him at all, since he is not pure of the first until the latter one heals.

notes.dh: מקמייתא טהר לי' לבתרייתא נטרי' ליה ז' ימי המשתה
notes.he: וא"ת והא בעי תגלחת וצפרים ואסור בתשמיש המטה כל ימי ספורו וי"ל כגון שלא היה אלא מצורע מוסגר א"נ אפילו מוחלט נהי דכי קצץ טמא מדרבנן מ"מ שרי לעשות תגלחת וצפרים ולמנות ימי ספורו וליטהר מן התורה ומיהו כפרתו א"א להביא דאינו יכול להכניס ידיו לבהונות כל זמן דטמא מדרבנן כדאמר (פסחים דף צב.) אע"פ שאין טבול יום אחר נכנס זה נכנס דלא התירו אלא משום פסח:
notes.en: From the first he has become pure; for the latter we wait the seven days of feasting: And if you say: but he still requires shaving and the birds, and is prohibited in marital relations all the days of his counting? One can say: for example, where he was only a quarantined leper. Alternatively, even a confirmed leper: granted that once he excised it he is impure by rabbinic law, he is nevertheless permitted to perform the shaving and the birds, to count his days of counting and to become pure by Torah law. But he cannot bring his atonement offerings, since he cannot put his hands into the Temple courtyard for the thumbs as long as he is impure by rabbinic law, as it says (Pesaḥim 92a): “Although a tevul yom does not enter otherwise, this one enters,” for they permitted it only for the Paschal offering.

notes.he: דלמפרע טהור משעת קציצה כלומר תעשה כמי שנטהר קודם שנולד בו נגע שני מן הראשון והיינו נותנין לו ז' ימי המשתה דחשבינן כמו השתא אתייליד לו נגע ולא קודם חתונתו דאי נולד לו קודם חתונתו לא היו נותנין לו והיינו דקאמר טומאה קמייתא טהר ליה טומאה דבתרייתא נטרינן ליה ז' ימי משתה:
notes.en: If you say we learned yit’har: that he is pure retroactively from the time of the excision, that is, he is treated as one who was purified of the first before the second mark developed in him, then we grant him the seven days of feasting, since we consider it as though the mark developed in him only now and not before his wedding; for had it developed before his wedding, they would not grant him [the days]. And this is what it says: of the first impurity he has become pure; for the latter impurity we wait for him the seven days of feasting.

messages.text: But if you say that we learned that the correct reading of Rabbi Eliezer’s statement is veyit’har, and the punitive impurity of the first mark remains intact until the ritual purity of the second mark has been confirmed, the grace period has no effect. The reason is that ultimately, even if the individual does not yet contract ritual impurity from the latter mark, he remains ritually impure on account of the first mark until the purification of the latter mark.

notes.he: כלומר דלא נטהר מן הראשונה אלא עכשיו כשנרפא הנגע השני סוף סוף כי לא מטמית ליה בבתריתא באותו שנולד בין חתונתו דיהבת ליה ז' ימי משתה מה מועיל ליה הא מטמי וקאי מקמייתא מנגע הראשון דהאי טומאה שייכא עד טהרה דנגע השני והוי טמא אפילו בימי המשתה:
notes.en: And if you say we learned veyit’har: that is, he becomes pure of the first only now, when the second mark is healed. Ultimately, though you do not declare him impure on account of the latter, the one that developed during his wedding, for which you grant him the seven days of feasting, what does it help him? He remains impure from the first mark, since that impurity applies until the purification of the second mark, and he is impure even during the days of feasting.

messages.text: What is the resolution to Rav Pappa’s query?

notes.he: מאי יטהר תנן או ויטהר תנן תיקו:
notes.en: What? Did we learn yit’har or did we learn veyit’har? Let it stand.

messages.text: Since there is no clear resolution, the dilemma shall stand unresolved.

@Rabbi Zeira In the case of one who slits the ear of a firstborn offering and subsequently dies, what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after the father’s death? Does the penalty prohibiting consumption of the firstborn offering extend to the son?
messages.lead: § The mishna teaches that one who slits the ear of a firstborn offering is prohibited indefinitely from slaughtering the animal on account of that blemish. Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma before Rabbi Zeira:
messages.quote: one who slits the ear of a firstborn offering, that person may never slaughter

notes.he: הצורם מהו לקנוס בנו אחריו שלא יאכל מאותו בכור עולמית:
notes.en: And dies: the one who slit it. What is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him, that he may never eat from that firstborn?

notes.dh: בעא מיניה ר' ירמיה מר' זירא צורם אוזן בכור ומת מהו שיקנסו בנו אחריו
notes.he: בפרק השולח (גיטין מד.) נקט תחלה הבעיא דמוכר עבדו ובמו"ק בפרק מי שהפך (מועד קטן דף יב:) נקט בכוון מלאכתו ובכל דוכתי עביד אם תימצי לומר מאידך ואכולהו פשיט תניתוה משדה שנתקווצה ואומר רבי דשלשתם שאל בבת אחת והש"ס קבע כל אחת במקומה כפי מה ששייכא ויש ספרים שכתוב במ"ק (שם) בעא מיניה רבא מר"נ אבל ברוב הספרים גרסינן ר' ירמיה מרבי זירא כמו כאן ובגיטין:
notes.en: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira: one who slits the ear of a firstborn and dies, do they penalize his son after him? In the chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 44a) the Gemara poses first the dilemma of one who sells his slave, and in Mo’ed Katan, in the chapter Mi SheHafakh (12b), that of one who planned his labor; everywhere it says “if you say” from the other cases, and it resolves them all with “You learned it” from the field whose thorns were removed. My teacher says that he asked all three at once, and the Talmud set each one in the place where it belongs. Some texts in Mo’ed Katan (ibid.) read “Rava asked Rav Naḥman,” but most texts read Rabbi Yirmeya asking Rabbi Zeira, as here and in Gittin.

messages.text: The Gemara compares this dilemma to two similar cases. If you say the halakha should be derived from the case of one who sells his Canaanite slave to gentiles and the seller subsequently dies, where the Sages penalized his son after the father’s death and required him to redeem the slave, this is not a direct parallel.

notes.he: במסכת גיטין דהמוכר עבדו לעובד כוכבים דקיימא לן קונסין אותו לפדותו עד עשרה בדמיו ומיבעיא לן התם אם מת המוכר מהו לקנוס בנו אחריו אם תימצי לומר ולמיפשט בההיא דקונסין התם דינא הוא דכל יומא מפקע ליה ממצות:
notes.en: If you say: in tractate Gittin, about one who sells his slave to a gentile, where we hold that we penalize him to redeem him for up to ten times his value, and there we raise the dilemma: if the seller died, what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him? If you say, and resolve that we penalize there, that is the law there, since every day he removes him from mitzvot.

notes.he: עסקינן בין בכהן בין בישראל כהן בבכור ודאי וישראל בספק בכור דנאכל לו במומו מהו שיקנסו בנו אחריו שיהא אסור לו (לוכל) [לאכול] קנסו בנו אחריו. לפדותו משום דכל יומא מפקע ליה ממצות אבל בבכור ליכא מפקע ולא קנסו:
notes.en: One who slits: we are dealing with either a priest or an Israelite: a priest with a certain firstborn, and an Israelite with an uncertain firstborn, which is eaten by him in its blemish. What is the halakha: do they penalize his son after him, so that it is forbidden to him to eat it? They penalized his son after him to redeem [the slave], since every day he removes him from mitzvot; but with a firstborn there is no such removal, and they did not penalize.

messages.text: It is possible that the penalty is extended to the son only there, as each day that the slave is in the servitude of the gentile master, that master prevents the slave from performing mitzvot. A Canaanite slave is obligated to perform the same mitzvot as a Jewish woman, and he is unable to fulfill the mitzvot when in the possession of a gentile. Since this reason does not apply in a case of a firstborn offering, the case of the Canaanite slave cannot be cited as a source to resolve this dilemma.

notes.dh: אם תמצא לומר מוכר עבדו לעובדי כוכבים ומת קנסו בנו אחריו דכל יומא מפקע ליה ממצות
notes.he: אכתי המ"ל דאפילו תימצי לומר התם לא קנסו (דדלמא) הכא קנסו משום דאיכא איסורא דאורייתא דכי האי גוונא איכא בפ' השולח גבי בעיא דמוכר עבדו ובמ"ק גבי בעיא דכוון מלאכתו במועד דקאמר אם תימצי לומר בצורם קנסו משום דאיכא אסורא דאורייתא ובגיטין נמי הוה מצי למינקט אם תימצי לומר לא קנסו הכא קנסו משום הפקעת מצות דכל יומא ויומא (כמו) בעבד ובמ"ק נמי נקט חד טעמא בצורם וטעמא אחרינא במוכר עבדו והוה מצי למימר חד טעמא בתרוייהו דאם תימצי לומר בצורם ובמוכר דקנסוה משום דעבדיה לאיסורא אבל כוון מלאכתו לא עבד לאיסורא:
notes.en: If you say: one who sells his slave to gentiles and dies, they penalized his son after him, since every day he removes him from mitzvot: One could still say that even if you say they did not penalize there, here they penalize, because there is a Torah prohibition; and so it is found in the chapter HaSholeaḥ, in the dilemma about one who sells his slave, and in Mo’ed Katan, in the dilemma about one who planned his labor on the Festival, where it says: “If you say they penalized one who slits, that is because there is a Torah prohibition.” In Gittin it could also have said: “If you say they did not penalize [one who slits], there they penalized because he removes him from mitzvot every day,” as with the slave. And in Mo’ed Katan too it gives one reason for one who slits and another for one who sells his slave, though it could have given one reason for both: “If you say they penalized one who slits and one who sells, because he committed a prohibited act; but one who planned his labor did not commit a prohibited act.”

messages.text: And if you say the halakha should be derived from the case of one who planned from the outset to perform his labor on the intermediate days of a Festival, by placing himself in a situation in which the labor should in theory be permitted, i.e., that a significant monetary loss would otherwise be incurred, that comparison is also inaccurate.

notes.he: הא דאמרינן במ"ק (דף יב:) המכוין מלאכתו במועד דמניח כרמו לבצור ואומר במועד אבצירנה שהרי דבר האבוד הוא והתירוהו חכמים במועד תאבד ולא יבצרנה הואיל ולכך נתכוין ומיבעיא לן התם אם מת קודם המועד מהו לקנוס בנו אחריו ולא יבצרנה במועד. ואם תימצי לומר התם הוא דלא קנסינן לבנו דהא לא עביד אביו איסורא דהא מת קודם המועד:
notes.en: And if you say: what we said in Mo’ed Katan (12b) about one who planned his labor for the Festival, who leaves his vineyard [unharvested] and says, “I will harvest it on the Festival, since it is a matter that would otherwise be lost, and the Sages permitted that on the Festival”: [there it is ruled that] it shall be lost and he shall not harvest it, since this is what he intended. And there we raise the dilemma: if he died before the Festival, what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him, so that he may not harvest it on the Festival? And if you say [that they did not penalize the son], it is there that we do not penalize his son, since his father did not commit a prohibited act, as he died before the Festival.

messages.text: In such a case the Sages penalized him by deeming it prohibited for him to perform the labor and by removing his rights to any of the finished products, but if he died before the start of the Festival, they did not penalize his son after the father’s death. This case is not a direct parallel either, as it is possible that it is only there that the penalty is not extended to the son, since the father did not yet perform a prohibited act, as he did not carry out any action on the Festival before he died.

notes.he: או אם תמצא לומר כיון מלאכתו במועד לא קנסו בנו כו' משום דמלאכת חולו של מועד מדרבנן אסור ולא מדאורייתא אסור:
notes.en: Or if you say: one who planned his labor on the Festival, they did not penalize his son, etc., since labor on the intermediate days of the Festival is prohibited by rabbinic law and not by Torah law.

messages.text: If so, here, in the case of mutilating the ear of a firstborn offering, what is the halakha? Should one say that the Sages penalized only him, i.e., the father, and he is no longer alive?

notes.he: עבד איסורא דמטיל מום בקדשים:
notes.en: But here: he committed a prohibited act, as he caused a blemish in consecrated animals.

messages.text: Or perhaps the Sages imposed the penalty upon his property, i.e., that no benefit may be derived from the animal, and that animal still exists in the possession of his heirs.

notes.he: לבכור:
notes.en: On his property: on the firstborn.

notes.he: או דלמא קנסוה לממוניה לבכור ולא יאכל אפילו לבנו:
notes.en: Or perhaps they penalized his property, the firstborn, so that he may not eat it, not even his son.

messages.text: @Rabbi Yirmeya You learned the resolution to your dilemma in a mishna:
messages.quote: what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son

messages.text: A field whose thorns were removed during the Sabbatical Year may be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year, as removing thorns is not full-fledged labor that renders the field prohibited.

notes.he: שנטל קוציה ממנה שהיו תלושין ומפוזרין בה:
notes.en: Whose thorns were removed: one took from it its thorns, which were detached and scattered over it.

notes.he: דליכא למיקנס מידי דהא לא עבד בשביעית עבודה חשובה:
notes.en: May be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year: since there is nothing to penalize, as he did not perform significant labor in the Sabbatical Year.

notes.he: פי' בקונט' שנטל קוצים ממנה שהיו תלושין ומפוזרין בה והדין עמו דא"א לומר בקוצים שהיו מחוברים דא"כ לא תזרע דאיכא איסורא דאורייתא בנטילתם שמייפה את הקרקע כדאמר שבת פרק הבונה (שבת דף קג.) גבי [התולש עולשין והמזרד זרדים] דבארעא דיליה חייב (בכל דיליה חייב) בכל שהוא משום דאיכא יפוי הקרקע דאפי' מתכוין לצורך דבר אחר וה"נ איכא יפוי קרקע כשתולש קוצים לחורשה לזריעה וכן משמע בירושלמי על המשנה תמן אסורים כשנטלו קוציה משמע דמוקי לה בתלושין:
notes.en: That was cleared of thorns: Rashi explained that one took from it thorns that were detached and scattered over it, and he is right. One cannot say it refers to attached thorns, for then it could not be sown, since removing them is a Torah prohibition, as it improves the ground, as stated in Shabbat, in the chapter HaBoneh (103a), about one who plucks endives or trims shoots: in his own land he is liable for any amount, because of the improvement of the ground, even if he intends it for another purpose. So too here, there is improvement of the ground when he plucks thorns in order to plow for sowing. And so it is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud on the mishna: “There they are prohibited when its thorns were removed,” which implies that it explains [our case] as detached thorns.

notes.he: שעקר הקוצים ממנה:
notes.en: Whose thorns were removed: one uprooted the thorns from it.

notes.he: דקוויץ לא חשיבה מלאכה:
notes.en: May be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year: since removing thorns is not considered labor.

messages.text: But if it had been improved with fertilizer, or if it had been enclosed so that the animals inside would fertilize it with their manure, it may not be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year, as both these acts cause significant improvements to the field. The Sages imposed a penalty that one may not derive benefit from prohibited labor.

notes.he: נזדבלה ע"י עגלות ומשואות של זבל:
notes.en: Had been improved: it was fertilized with wagons and loads of manure.

notes.he: על ידי דיר בהמות שמעמידין ומשכיבין אותה חדש או חדשים כדי לזבלה:
notes.en: Had been enclosed: by means of a pen for animals, which are stood and bedded down in it for a month or two in order to fertilize it.

notes.he: דקנסינן דעבד עבודה חשובה בשביעית:
notes.en: It may not be sown: since we penalize him, as he performed significant labor in the Sabbatical Year.

notes.he: בירושלמי מפרש איזהו טיוב כל העם פעם אחת חורשין והוא חורש שתי פעמים:
notes.en: Had been improved: in the Jerusalem Talmud it explains: what is improvement? Everyone plows once, and he plows twice.

notes.he: שניזדבלה בשביעית או מדיירה. שהביא שם בהמות לזבלה בשביעית הוה חשיבה מלאכה דהיינו תולדה דחרישה לא תזרע למוצאי שביעית:
notes.en: Had been improved: it was fertilized in the Sabbatical Year; or had been enclosed: he brought animals there to fertilize it in the Sabbatical Year. This is considered labor, being a subcategory of plowing; it may not be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year.

messages.text: And Rav Asi, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, says: We have a tradition that if one improved his field in a prohibited manner and then died, his son may sow it.

notes.he: אם האי טיוב מדרבנן קשה היכי פשיט צורם אוזן בכור דאורייתא ואם הוא נמי דאורייתא קשה בגיטין (דף מד:) דפשיט מיניה גבי עבד (עברי) לימא שאני הכא דחמיר משום דמפקע ליה ממצות וי"ל דקסבר שראוי להחמיר בשביעית יותר מכולם כדאמר בקדושין (דף כ.) כמה קשה אבקה של שביעית:
notes.en: If one improved it and died, his son may sow it: If this improvement is prohibited by rabbinic law, it is difficult: how does it resolve the case of one who slits the ear of a firstborn, which is by Torah law? And if it too is by Torah law, it is difficult in Gittin (44b), which resolves from it the case of the slave: let one say that it is different there, since it is more severe, as he removes him from mitzvot. One can say that he holds it is fitting to be more stringent with the Sabbatical Year than with all of them, as it says in Kiddushin (20a): How severe is even the dust of the Sabbatical Year.

notes.he: הטיבה בשביעית ומת בנו זורעה למוצאי שביעית:
notes.en: If he improved it in the Sabbatical Year and died, his son may sow it at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year.

messages.text: Apparently, the Sages penalized only him, i.e., the father, but the Sages did not penalize his son.
We have a tradition…

Abaye’s tradition continues on 35a: if one rendered impure the ritually pure items of another and died, the Sages did not penalize his son, since damage that is not evident is not considered damage by Torah law.
